topic.title: The counteroffer
topic.claim: Your counteroffer is the raise you were never offered: the day you resign, the budget appears.
topic.moment: Asking for a raise twice and hearing 'next cycle', then a meeting with a number two days after resigning.

turn.believed: a counteroffer means the company values you
turn.actually: it's a correction: the price of keeping you, paid only when replacing you costs more

topic.because: as long as you stay quiet, the cheapest raise is none; a resignation changes the company's sum, not your worth
topic.payoff: The real appraisal calendar has three dates: March, September, and the day you resign. Only one comes with a number.

cover.headline: Funny how "budgets are tight" lasts exactly until you [resign.]
cover.sub: Then a number shows up within two days.

paragraphs: Funny how "budgets are tight" lasts exactly until you resign. Then a number shows up within two days.
slides.why_swipe: everyone has heard 'budgets are tight'; where does the money suddenly come from?

paragraphs: March appraisal: "tough year, next cycle pakka." September: the same line, on a new slide deck.
Then you resign on a Monday. By Wednesday there's a Teams invite called "Quick chat", and suddenly there's a number on the table.
slides.why_swipe: the scene is familiar; why does the money appear only now?

paragraphs: I've seen this play out in almost every office I've been around. They always wanted to keep you.
They just wanted to keep you for free, and as long as asking was all you did, free worked.
slides.why_swipe: the motive is out; so what is that number, really?

paragraphs: The money usually isn't from your manager's budget either. It tends to sit in a retention pot that nobody mentions until someone puts in their papers.
**That number isn't a reward. It's arrears.**
slides.why_swipe: the turn has landed; how does it feel to be on the receiving end?

paragraphs: You feel flattered for about an hour. Then you do the maths on the last two years.
And if you take it, they now know your exit price. Your manager can't quite look at you in that meeting.
slides.why_swipe: the feeling is out; what's the real lesson about appraisals?

paragraphs: The real appraisal calendar in most Indian offices has three dates: March, September, and the day you resign.
**Only one of them comes with a number.**

end.save: Read it again before your next "next cycle" conversation.
end.send: Send it to the colleague who's heard "next cycle pakka" twice.

draft.caption: Be it March or September, what's the most creative way you've been told "next cycle"?
draft.alt_text: A text carousel arguing that a counteroffer is the raise you were never offered: companies find the budget only when replacing you would cost more.

history.note: opinion-first sample reviewed by the owner on 2026-10-23

Money offered in a resignation-triggered.correct: Practice is mixed and not well-documented by primary or major-outlet sources. Some employers maintain a separate 'retention'/market-adjustment budget distinct from the manager's merit budget (compensation-consulting guidance recommends this), but other accounts describe managers simply finding money from their own team/cost-center budget once a resignation lands ('the budget appears within 48 hours'), and having a dedicated retention budget is described as increasing (not guaranteeing) the odds of a counteroffer being made at all. No SHRM, HBR, or similar authoritative source confirms which funding source is 'typical' across employers, so the claim as a general rule cannot be verified or disproven with reliable evidence.

sources.quote: A retention budget funds a specific, documented talent risk and should not quietly consume the pool approved for the broader workforce... Some smaller companies run one pool for merit, market adjustments and retention, so a higher number can include a counteroffer for someone who was about to leave.
When a manager has retention budget, the counter-offer likelihood is 90%+.

[Article discusses counteroffer pay caps as 'not taking too many resources away from the department or the company overall' but does not identify a separate dedicated retention budget as the typical funding source.]

In most Indian offices, the effective ap.correct: The exact month varies by company rather than being literally 'March and September' everywhere: most large Indian employers (e.g., TCS) run their core cycle on the April 1–March 31 financial year, with ratings/decisions finalized around January–March and raises taking effect April 1 — TCS returned to this 'usual appraisal timeline' for 2026, effective April 1. A second cycle genuinely exists at major employers around Q3 (e.g., TCS's delayed FY25 hikes were rolled out September 1, 2025; Infosys runs an October-to-September review calendar; HCLTech's H2 rewards go into effect October 1), so 'September' is a reasonable shorthand for this second wave even though the precise month differs by firm. The third 'date' — a resignation triggering a raise/counteroffer — is well documented: India's attrition and counteroffer data (foundit's 2025 Appraisal Trends Report) show most employees who received hikes still plan to switch, underscoring how central resignation-driven negotiation is to actual pay movement in Indian offices. Overall framing holds as a fair characterization, with company-level variation in exact months.

sources.quote: The move marks a return to TCS's usual appraisal timeline after salary hikes in the previous cycle were deferred by five months and implemented in September 2025.
We will be issuing wage hikes to around 80% of our employees effective September 1, 2025.
74% of employees received an increment in the FY24–25 cycle, [yet] 86% are still planning to change jobs in the coming months.

notes: The take's premise is wrong: The premise that a fast counteroffer proves the appraisal-era 'budgets are tight' was a lie about the same pot of money. The post treats one budget where there are two. Merit/increment budgets and retention budgets are set and justified separately, so a counteroffer existing does not mean a raise was being withheld from a scarce-but-available appraisal budget. Notably, the post's own slide 4 ('it sits in a retention pot that nobody mentions') is the correct fact that actually defeats its conclusion.. How it actually works: Annual merit/increment budgets are fixed top-down months in advance as a small percent of payroll (India's 2026 average is ~9.1%, and the core merit component is typically only 3-4%), and employers deliberately ring-fence separate retention/market-correction pools so those don't compress the merit pool — so 'the merit budget is tight' can be literally true at appraisal time. A resignation doesn't unlock withheld arrears; it supplies a credible outside number that flips the comparison from 'merit raise vs. an employee who is staying anyway' to 'retention payment vs. replacement cost,' and replacement runs 50-200% of annual salary (Gallup/SHRM). The counteroffer is a forward-looking cost-avoidance payment drawn on a different budget and justified by a different calculation, not back-pay the company was secretly pocketing. Rebuild the post on the correct mechanism.

Could not verify: 'Money offered in a resignation-triggered counteroffer typically comes from a dedicated retention budget/pot rather than the departing employee's manager's regular budget.'. Cut it, or state it only if a source says it.

ledger.text: Because companies can and do produce a monetary counteroffer quickly once an employee resigns, the 'budgets are tight' reasoning given during scheduled appraisal cycles is not true scarcity but a withheld raise that is only released under the threat of departure.

sources.quote: Salaries in India are projected to increase by 9.1% in 2026... based on data from over 1,060 companies across 45 industries.
Average increment in India is expected to be 9.1 percent in 2026, compared with 9.0 percent in 2025.
Budgets can be allocated top-down from a total pool... pool amounts are calculated and can be adjusted using the Top-Down option — merit budgets are a fixed, pre-set pool, not open-ended.
Separate pools for retention adjustments or market corrections prevent those decisions from compressing the core merit pool — retention money is budgeted apart from the merit/appraisal budget.
The cost of replacing an employee can range from 50% to 200% of their annual salary, depending on their level — the number a counteroffer is weighed against is replacement cost, not the merit budget.
